newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Britain calls Burma a "nasty, dictatorial regime".
newsitem.headline: Britain calls Burma a "nasty, dictatorial regime".

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said on Wednesday the Burmese military government was a "rather nasty, dictatorial regime" but declined to call for its international isolation.

Rifkind, in Singapore for talks between ministers from the seven-nation Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and the European Union (EU), praised Burmese opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi and her efforts to bring democracy to the country.
But he told a meeting of local academics there was no point singling out Burma as if it were the only problem the international community faced.
"Burma is not the only example in the world of a rather nasty, dictatorial regime. There are sadly other countries of a similar characteristic," he said.

Burma is expected to be a key issue at the ASEAN-EU meetings with European politicians facing pressure back home since last year's crackdown by Burma's military government on the country's pro-democracy movement.

The London-based human rights group Amnesty International said on Wednesday that political repression and human rights violations in Burma last year reached their highest levels since the suppression of a popular uprising at the end of the 1980s.
In a report, Amnesty also called on ASEAN to end its policy of "constructive engagement" with Rangoon.
Asked if Britain supported Amnesty's call for an end to the policy, Rifkind told a news conference earlier on Wednesday:
"It is a matter for ASEAN to decide what relationship it wishes to have with Burma."
"We have sought to impress upon the government in Rangoon the need to initiate democratic reforms and to open up their society," he told reporters.
ASEAN groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
ASEAN, which says constructive engagement will bring about reforms in Burma, has agreed to admit Burma as a member along with Laos and Cambodia some time in the future.
But the Amnesty report said ASEAN countries needed to think again about how to press the Burmese authorities to improve their human rights record.
Burma's military government dismissed the Amnesty report on its human rights record as "ridiculous", and said it was propaganda for anti-Burmese organisations.
Rifkind told the academics there was wide concern about the situation in the country.

"This is a very great tribute due to Aung San Suu Kyi. She is a remarkable lady. She clearly speaks for a very large number of Burmese people, perhaps a large majority of the people of that country," he said.
"We do need to look at ways of helping those who are struggling for a more open and a more democratic society in Burma to realise that aspiration."
But he added: "Each country must come to its own judgement as to whether it wishes to try to help in that process or not."
